clinicalPearls: An umbrella term for mosaic neurocutaneous disorders in which epidermal naevi are associated with extracutaneous abnormalities of the central nervous system, eyes and skeleton.
Arises from post-zygotic somatic mutations producing genetic mosaicism, so the naevi follow the lines of Blaschko.

Several distinct entities are recognised, including Schimmelpenning syndrome with naevus sebaceus, naevus comedonicus syndrome, CHILD syndrome, Becker naevus syndrome and phakomatosis pigmentokeratotica.
Common driver mutations involve the RAS-MAPK pathway (HRAS, KRAS, NRAS) and FGFR3, with PIK3CA in some overgrowth phenotypes.
Neurological features include seizures, developmental delay, intellectual disability and hemimegalencephaly.
Ocular findings include colobomas, lipodermoids and choristomas, while skeletal features include scoliosis and limb hypoplasia.
Naevus sebaceus carries a small risk of secondary benign and, less often, malignant tumours in adulthood.
Management is multidisciplinary and directed at the specific systems involved.
reference.pathophysiology: Epidermal naevus syndromes result from post-zygotic somatic activating mutations, most often in RAS-MAPK pathway genes or FGFR3, present in a mosaic distribution. Cells carrying the mutation populate ectodermally derived tissues along embryonic migration lines, producing epidermal naevi and, where the mutation affects neural, ocular or skeletal precursors, corresponding extracutaneous malformations. The pattern and severity depend on the timing and lineage of the mutational event.
additionalDifferentials: Other neurocutaneous syndromes (tuberous sclerosis, neurofibromatosis, incontinentia pigmenti)
Proteus syndrome and PIK3CA-related overgrowth spectrum
Isolated naevus sebaceus without systemic involvement
additionalInvestigations: Skin examination and biopsy of naevi with histopathology
MRI brain for hemimegalencephaly and other malformations
Skeletal survey or targeted imaging for deformity
Molecular testing of affected lesional tissue for mosaic mutations
Renal and other organ imaging guided by phenotype
redFlags: Rapid growth, ulceration or change within a naevus suggesting tumour transformation
reference.prognosis: Highly variable and dependent on the extent of extracutaneous involvement; isolated cutaneous disease has an excellent outlook, whereas extensive central nervous system involvement carries a risk of intractable epilepsy and intellectual disability.
pitfalls: Regarding epidermal naevi as purely cosmetic and missing systemic associations.
Testing blood rather than lesional tissue for the mosaic mutation.
Overlooking the small malignant potential of naevus sebaceus.
references: Consensus guidance on mosaic RASopathies and epidermal naevi
management: Anticonvulsant therapy for seizures, with epilepsy surgery such as hemispherectomy considered for intractable epilepsy from hemimegalencephaly
Dermatological treatment of epidermal naevi using topical agents, laser or surgical excision for symptomatic or disfiguring lesions
Developmental support, early intervention and tailored educational provision for developmental delay and intellectual disability
Ophthalmology assessment and management of colobomas, lipodermoids and choristomas
Orthopaedic management of scoliosis and limb deformity or hypoplasia
Emerging targeted therapy directed at the RAS-MAPK or PIK3CA pathway, such as MEK inhibitors, in selected severe or overgrowth phenotypes
Surveillance for tumours arising within naevus sebaceus and for evolving neurological and skeletal complications
Multidisciplinary neurocutaneous care with genetic counselling, noting the mosaic somatic origin and generally low recurrence risk
